Ilza Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Iłża, Poland

Demolished. Jews in Iłża first appear in records in the second half of the 18th century, with a kehilla by 1765 and synagogue supervision from 1850. Before 1837, the town's Jews were buried 21 km away in Sienna; a cholera outbreak that year prompted the community to establish its own epidemic cemetery, formally authorized by the state in 1840 and fenced within two years. By 1921, Iłża's 1,545 Jewish residents made up over a third of the population; most were murdered at Treblinka in October 1942, and the cemetery's tombstones and fence were destroyed during the war. Poland ordered the site closed in 1964, citing 1943 as the year of its last burial. In 2006, descendants of Iłża's Jews funded a restoration: the cemetery was refenced, cleared, and a Holocaust memorial and information board were installed.
